role.altitude: The reporter keeps choosing stories, being at the scene, interviewing and writing opinion; scanning duplicate items, typing subtitles and fixing spelling and house style by hand shrink.
skills_to_grow: Keeping beat filters, the names list and house style rules current
role.ambitious_version: A reporter who turns most own stories into radio scripts and video with subtitles without extra evenings.

tasks.short: Scan wire copy, press releases and other sources for news, check what was already published, pitch topics in the editorial meeting and take assignments from the editor.

steps.what: Reporter examines grouped news items from the wire, press releases, council agendas and other outlets

loop.input: Wire items, public press releases and agenda items that passed the reporter's beat filters (keywords, places, organisations).
loop.output: Groups of items about the same event, each with a one-line summary and links to every item in the group.
loop.check: Every summary must repeat a fact from the lead of at least one linked item, or it is replaced by that lead; every item keeps its link. Before picking a topic the reporter reads the leads behind its group and checks the summary says what they say, and opens the originals of any topic picked.
loop.stop: One grouping pass per feed refresh; items it cannot place stay ungrouped in the list.
loop.why_not_simpler: Keyword filters cut the volume, but the same event arrives from the wire, a press office and an agenda in different words.

steps.what: Reporter picks the topics to address
Reporter searches the archive to see what the outlet already published on each topic
Reporter pitches topics in the editorial meeting and obtains assignments from the editor
Desk editor puts the assignments on the news planning board
Reporter reads the assignment and background and plans the first calls

tasks.design: A monitoring view filters the wire, public press releases and agendas by the reporter's beat rules, and a bounded step groups items about the same event with a one-line summary and links, checked against each item's lead. Each group shows earlier coverage from an archive search in the {CMS} on its names and places. Picking topics, the editorial meeting and planning calls stay with the reporter; tips from sources stay in the reporter's own mailbox and never enter the tool.
tasks.previous_blocker: The same event arrived from several sources in different words, so every item had to be read to find what was new.
tasks.enabler_now: Monitoring tools filter feeds by topic, and language models can group differently worded items about one event.
tasks.still_hard: Judging what is news for this audience today.
tasks.human_edge: Knowing which small item hides a story and which source to call first.
tasks.altitude: The reporter spends less of the morning reading duplicates and more on calls; decision rights do not change.

reach.learn: Whether grouped items with earlier coverage make the morning meeting shorter.

evidence.claim: Monitoring tools track news topics and conversations across sources.
Language models can group news items that describe the same event in different words.
The national journalists' model guideline says no confidential or personal data goes into AI tools.

assumptions: Boundary: from incoming items to a reporting plan; reporting and writing are outside.

Input contract for s1: wire items from the agency feed, press releases from the shared newsroom mailbox, public agendas from council sites; the beat filters are kept by the reporter; fallback is reading the full feed.
Only public material enters the grouping step; tips and source mail are excluded.
Coverage: about 70% of incoming items come through the feed and the shared mailbox; s1 is priced at that share.
The editorial meeting and the editor's planning do not change.
Pricing of s1: filtering by beat rules and grouping items about the same event cut the reading by about 40%; the reporter still reads each relevant group.
unknowns: How many items per day reach the reporter's beat.
Whether the archive search is reachable from outside the CMS.
research_questions: How often does grouping merge two different events?
Does the reporter miss items that the filters drop?

already_counted.description: Reporter reads grouped items and opens originals of picked topics.
Reporter reads the earlier coverage links.

incremental.description: Reporter tunes beat filters when sources or topics change.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: a general news reporter whose filters let most items through (s1 80, s3 80) (6.3); high: a council or courts reporter with many duplicate items (14.7).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Take pictures or video at the scene, note names, transfer and select files, edit photos and cut clips, add subtitles, write captions and attach the media to the story.

steps.what: Reporter takes pictures or video at the scene
Reporter asks people pictured for their names and agreement and notes them
Reporter transfers files from camera or phone into the media library
Reporter selects the best shots
Reporter processes photos (crop, exposure) and cuts video clips
Reporter types subtitles for video clips

loop.input: The audio track of each cut clip and the names list from the scene.
loop.output: A timed subtitle file in the house subtitle format.
loop.check: Names in the subtitles must match the names list or are marked; the reporter plays the clip with subtitles and corrects every line before it is attached.
loop.stop: One transcription per cut; a new cut means a new run.
loop.why_not_simpler: Typing subtitles by hand takes several times the clip length; there is no rule that turns speech into text.

steps.what: Reporter writes captions and metadata: names, place, date and credit
Reporter uploads the media to the CMS and attaches it to the story

tasks.design: Files from the camera or phone import straight into the {CMS} media library with date, place and credit from the file metadata, so transfer, upload and most caption fields are not typed. Editing presets handle routine crops and exposure; a speech-to-text service drafts subtitles that the reporter checks line by line against the clip and the names list from the scene. Shooting, asking names, choosing shots and writing caption text stay with the reporter; no generative edits are made to news images.
tasks.previous_blocker: Files moved by card and upload, captions were typed field by field, and subtitles were typed by hand.
tasks.enabler_now: Media libraries import from phones and cameras with metadata; Dutch speech-to-text is good enough to correct rather than type.
tasks.still_hard: Being in the right place and getting the shot; names spoken on site must still be written down.
tasks.human_edge: Seeing the picture that tells the story and getting people's agreement on the spot.

ambition.what: Short subtitled video with most stories, not only the big ones.

tasks.altitude: The reporter spends the saved time at the scene or on the story; decision rights do not change.

reach.task: Deliver captioned photos to the desk
reach.learn: Whether metadata import keeps credits and dates right without typing.

evidence.claim: A Dutch speech-to-text service sells machine subtitles stated as over 90% accurate and human-checked ones over 99%.
Generated or manipulated audio and video must be disclosed; the design makes no generative edits.

assumptions: Boundary: from shooting at the scene to media attached to the story; the editor's choice and publication are outside.
Input contract for s7: date, place and credit from the file metadata, written by the camera or phone; names come only from the reporter's names list from the scene; fallback is typing all fields.
Captions carry the actual names and places recorded on site, not those in the assignment.
Coverage: about 40% of stories carry a video clip; the subtitle saving applies only to those, which is already inside s6's share.
Shooting and asking names do not change.
Pricing of s5: presets handle routine crops and exposure only, about a tenth of the step; cutting video clips does not change.
unknowns: Whether the CMS media library accepts direct phone import.
research_questions: How many subtitle lines need correction per minute of clip?
Does subtitled video reach more readers?

already_counted.description: Reporter corrects drafted subtitles against the clip.
Reporter checks imported caption fields and writes caption text.

incremental.description: Reporter keeps editing presets and the subtitle format current.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: a print story with a few photos and no video, so subtitles do not apply and captions are mostly typed (s6 100, s7 80) (8.7); high: a video story with several interviews (13.3).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Check facts, names and quotes in the copy, correct spelling, grammar and punctuation, apply house style, fit the length, review audio and video against the script, and file to the desk for the final check.

steps.what: Reporter reviews written copy for errors in content: names, numbers and quotes against notes and recordings
Reporter corrects spelling, grammar and punctuation
Reporter applies the prescribed editorial style: numbers, titles, abbreviations and spelling of names
Reporter measures the copy's length or reading time against the slot
Reporter cuts the copy to fit the length or air time of the slot
Reporter reviews audio or video copy by listening to the cut against the script
Reporter files the corrected copy to the desk and answers its questions
Desk editor does the final check of the filed copy

tasks.design: In the {CMS} editor, a quote check marks every quoted sentence that does not appear in the reporter's interview transcripts, and names are matched against the story's names list, so the reporter rechecks only marked items. A spelling and grammar checker and house style rules with a term list run as suggestions the reporter accepts one by one, and the editor shows length or reading time for the slot. Listening to cuts, deciding what to fix and the desk's final check stay with people; filing moves from e-mail to a {CMS} status.
tasks.previous_blocker: Style rules lived in a PDF guide and quotes were checked by scrolling through notes.
tasks.enabler_now: Dutch spelling and style checkers run inside editors; machine transcripts of interviews make quotes searchable.
tasks.still_hard: Quotes from unrecorded phone calls and facts that need a second source.
tasks.human_edge: Knowing when a correct sentence still says the wrong thing.
tasks.altitude: The reporter spends checking time on facts that matter instead of commas; decision rights do not change.

reach.learn: Which style rules reporters reject most, and whether the guide or the rule is wrong.

evidence.claim: A proofreading tool checks Dutch spelling, grammar, punctuation and style.
A style tool scores text against a house style guide repeatably, with quality gates.
The national journalists' model guideline asks for a final check by another person.

assumptions: Boundary: from the reporter's draft to copy cleared by the desk; publication is outside.
Input contract for s1: interview transcripts made from the reporter's own recordings and a names list per story kept by the reporter; fallback is checking notes by hand.
Coverage: about 60% of quotes come from recorded interviews; the s1 saving is priced at that share.
Checkers only suggest; no model rewrites the copy.
Listening to cuts and the desk's final check do not change.

s2 keeps 60: the checker catches most slips, but the reporter still reads the copy because wrong words that are spelled right pass it. In s1 the reporter still checks that each matched quote is used in its context.
unknowns: Whether interviews are recorded and transcribed today.
How complete the house style guide is as rules.
research_questions: How many errors reach the desk before and after the checkers?
How many quote marks are false alarms?

already_counted.description: Reporter rechecks marked quotes and names and the unrecorded quotes.
Reporter accepts or rejects spelling, grammar and style suggestions.

incremental.description: Reporter adds new names and terms to the term list and reports wrong style rules.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: copy with many quotes from unrecorded calls and new names (s1 90, s2 70) (24.7); high: routine copy from recorded interviews (33.7).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Choose the angle and gather material, write the commentary or column, turn own reporting into broadcast scripts, check facts and quotes, revise after the editor's comments, and get it approved and published.

steps.what: Reporter chooses the angle of the commentary or column
Reporter gathers material from notes, earlier reporting and data

loop.input: The reporter's question and the outlet's own archive.
loop.output: A short list of earlier articles that answer it, each with the quoted passage and a link.
loop.check: Every quoted passage must be found word for word in the linked article, or the item is dropped. The reporter reads the linked articles before using them and checks each passage supports the point it is used for.
loop.stop: One answer per question; no follow-up runs without a new question.
loop.why_not_simpler: Keyword search returns many articles; the reporter needs the passage that answers the question.

steps.what: Reporter writes the commentary or column using the computer
Reporter writes broadcast scripts from own published reporting

loop.input: The reporter's own published article and the house radio script template with target reading time.
loop.output: A draft spoken-word script with short sentences, within the reading time.
loop.check: Every name, number and quote must match the source article, or the line is marked; nothing absent from the article is allowed. The reporter reads the script against the article (same meaning, no lost qualifier), edits it and reads it aloud for timing.
loop.stop: One draft per article version; if rejected, the reporter writes the script.
loop.why_not_simpler: A template sets the length; turning written sentences into spoken ones needs rewriting.

steps.what: Reporter checks facts and quotes in the commentary and scripts
Reporter revises the piece after the editor's comments
Desk editor reads the final piece and scripts and approves them for publication
Desk editor publishes the commentary or column in the CMS at its slot

approvals.approved_version: final piece as approved in s7; the scheduled publication uses that version and any later edit voids it

tasks.design: An answer desk over the outlet's own archive in the {CMS} returns earlier articles with quoted passages, checked word for word, for the reporter to read. For broadcast, a bounded step drafts a spoken-word script from the reporter's own published article in the house template, with every name, number and quote matched to the article; the reporter edits and times it. Commentaries and columns are written by the reporter, facts are checked with the same quote and names check as other copy, and the desk editor approves the final version, which the {CMS} publishes at its slot.
tasks.previous_blocker: Scripts were rewritten from articles by hand, and earlier coverage was found by keyword search through many results.
tasks.enabler_now: Language models rewrite text into spoken style, and each fact can be checked against the source article.
tasks.still_hard: Opinion and voice; drafting commentary with a model risks invented quotes and is not done.
tasks.human_edge: A view readers trust, written in the reporter's own voice.

ambition.what: Radio listeners get scripts from stories that today only appear in print or online.

tasks.altitude: The reporter writes the commentary as before and spends less time rewriting for radio; decision rights do not change.

reach.learn: Whether drafted scripts read naturally or need presenter rewrites.

evidence.claim: A news agency is testing turning articles into radio scripts with a university lab.
A former editor was suspended for AI-invented quotes in 15 of 53 blog posts, which is why commentary is not drafted by a model.
Public-interest text made with AI needs a label unless a person reviews it under editorial responsibility.

assumptions: Boundary: from the angle to the approved piece published, or the approved script filed to the studio rundown; reading on air is outside.

Input contract for s4: only the reporter's own published article is used as source; the house script template with reading time per slot is kept by the radio desk; fallback is writing the script by hand.
The editor's final check under editorial responsibility covers drafted scripts, so no AI label is needed; this is an assumption to confirm with the outlet's editorial council.
Coverage: about half of the reporter's articles also need a broadcast script; s4 is priced at that share.
Writing the commentary, revisions and the editor's review do not change.
Pricing of s2: earlier reporting is about a third of gathering for a commentary; the archive desk saves about 60% of that part; gathering from notes and data does not change.
unknowns: Share of the reporter's work that goes to radio or TV.
Whether the archive is open to a search tool under the outlet's rights.
research_questions: How many lines of a drafted script survive the reporter's edit?
Do listeners notice a difference in drafted scripts?

already_counted.description: Reporter edits and times drafted scripts.
Reporter reads archive passages before using them.

incremental.description: Reporter keeps the script template and pronunciation notes current with the radio desk.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: a columnist writing opinion pieces only, with no broadcast scripts (s4 100) (4.6); high: about half of articles also become radio scripts (10.9).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional
